q:
Which of the following statements regarding Nannaya Bhattu are correct?
I. Nannaya Bhattu was a Telugu poet who translated the Sanskrit Mahabharata into Telugu as ' Andhra Mahabharatam '.
II. He is also credited with writing ' Andhra Shabda Chintamani ', a Sanskrit treatise on Telugu grammar.
III. Raja Raja Narendra donated Nandampudi Agrahara to Nannaya.
explanation:
Official key: I and III (Nandampudi to Nannaya). Strictly: the Nandampudi grant names Narayana Bhattu as donee and Nannaya as its composer, so I and II (NextGen Eastern Chalukyas p.20, p.33).
Statements I and II are right: Nannaya translated the Mahabharata (Andhra Mahabharatam) and is credited with Andhra Shabda Chintamani. Statement III is wrong, because Rajaraja Narendra gave Nandampudi to Narayana Bhattu and Nannaya only composed the grant (official key: I and III).

notes.text: - **Oldest** spoken and literary language of South India = **Tamil** (Polytechnic Lecturers 2012); Tamil got classical status first (2004).

q: Who spread Veerashaivism in Andhra?
explanation:
Some keys: Basava (founder of Veerashaivism) or Somanatha (who popularised it in Telugu). Strictly: Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya propagated it in Andhra (NextGen Andhra Cholas p.3).
Veerashaivism was spread in Andhra by Mallikarjuna Panditaradhya (12th c.); Basava founded it in Karnataka, and Palkuriki Somanatha later popularised it through Telugu literature. The printed key (Basava) contradicts its own explanation.

q: The conquest of South India was completed during the reign of:
explanation: Alauddin began the southern expeditions through Malik Kafur, but under Muhammad bin Tughlaq the south was annexed and the Sultanate reached its greatest extent, down to Madurai (Ma'bar).

q: The Delhi Sultan who established a Ministry of Agriculture was:
explanation: Muhammad bin Tughlaq set up the Diwan-i-Amir-i-Kohi, a department (ministry) of agriculture to extend cultivation.

q: Identify the Sultan of Delhi who prohibited drinking of alcohol, introduced market control policy and inflicted severe punishment to rapists.
explanation: Alauddin Khalji prohibited liquor, introduced market (price) control and punished offenders severely; Firuz Tughlaq and Iltutmish are not linked with market control.

notes.text: - **MBT** was the **first Sultan to join the public celebration of Holi**; consorted with jogis and Jain monk **Jinaprabha Suri**; visited the Ajmer shrine.

q: Which system of transport was often used by the Delhi Sultanate to transport fruits of Khorasan to India?
explanation: Ibn Battuta says the foot-post (dawa), quicker than the horse-post (ulaq), was often used to carry the fruits of Khurasan, much desired in India.

notes.text: - **Post (Ibn Battuta):** **ulaq** = **horse post**; **dawa** = **foot post** (runners every third of a mile) – the **foot post, quicker than the horse post, was often used to bring the fruits of Khurasan** to India. **Dak chowki** = Sher Shah. **Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq** improved the post with runners and horsemen.

q: What is the name of the tax levied by Aurangzeb on Non-Muslim subjects of his kingdom?
explanation: Aurangzeb reimposed jizya, the tax on non-Muslims, in 1679; zakat and ushr were paid by Muslims and khums was the share of booty.

State's share of 1 / 5th of the war booty
key_text: State's share of 1 / 5th of the war booty
explanation: Khams (khums) was the state's one-fifth share of war booty.

q:
Consider the following statements

A. Shamsudin Iltutmish was the first sultan of Delhi to issue regular currency and to declare Delhi as the capital of his empire

B. Shamsudin Iltutmish set up the Iqtadari system which means division of empire into Iqtas, which were assigned to the nobles and officers in lieu of salary

C. Shamsudin Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and the copper Jital, two basic coins of sultanate period, with a standard weight of 175gm
Which of the above statement is/are correct?
explanation:
NextGen and this paper write '175 gm'. Strictly the tanka weighed 175 grains (about 11 g), so C is literally wrong; read as grains, all three are correct.
Intended key 'All of these': Iltutmish issued regular currency and made Delhi the capital (A), set up the iqtadari system (B) and introduced the silver tanka and copper jital (C).

notes.text: - **MBT** raised taxes in the **Doab** during a famine; neither Alauddin nor MBT took one-sixth – so "one-sixth" statements are **false** (CDS 2005).

q: Who introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital - the two basic coins of the Sultanate period ?
explanation: Iltutmish introduced the silver tanka and the copper jital, the two basic coins of the Sultanate.

notes.text: - **Alauddin** held a religious discourse with the Jain **Acharya Mahasena** (Jain tradition) – CDS 2005 statement I true.

q: The term 'Delhiwal' in the medieval history is associated with
options: Coins that were minted in Delhi
Taxes collected on Agriculture by rulers
Export of Spices, textiles and Indigo from Delhi
key_text: Coins that were minted in Delhi
explanation: Dehliwal (Delhiwal) was a coin minted at Delhi, current in the Sultanate period (also under the Rajput Chauhans and Tomaras), not a tax or an export.

notes.text: - **NDA 2002:** Alauddin **fixed grain prices**, **paid soldiers in cash** and **raised revenue to half** – all three correct.

q: Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque in Delhi was built by:
explanation: Qutbuddin Aibak built the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque (completed 1198), the first mosque of the Turkish rulers in Delhi, from the material of 27 temples.

q: The Qutab Minar was named after: merican
explanation:
Most books and keys: named after Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki. Some historians: named after its builder Qutbuddin Aibak (Wikipedia, citing ASI).
The Qutb Minar is commonly held to be named after the Sufi saint Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki; it was begun by Qutbuddin Aibak and completed by Iltutmish. Iltutmish and Raziya are not its namesakes.

notes.text: - **Name:** commonly believed to honour Sufi saint **Khwaja Qutbuddin Bakhtiyar Kaki** (⚠ debated: some say Aibak).

q:
Match the following authors with their works:
List I
List II
a. Al-Biruni
I. Tariqh-i-Firoz Shahi
b. Minhaj-us-Siraj
II. Tahqiq-i-Hind
c. Ziauddin Barani
III. The Rihla
d. Ibn Battuta
IV. Tabaqat-i-Nasiri
explanation: Al-Biruni – Tahqiq-i-Hind (II); Minhaj-us-Siraj – Tabaqat-i-Nasiri (IV); Barani – Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi (I); Ibn Battuta – Rihla (III). So a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III.

notes.text: - **APPSC G1 match:** Al-Biruni – **Tahqiq-i-Hind**; Minhaj – **Tabaqat-i-Nasiri**; Barani – **Tarikh-i-Firoz Shahi**; Ibn Battuta – **Rihla** → a-II, b-IV, c-I, d-III.

q: Who shifted the capital of the Bahmani Kingdom from Gulbarga to Bidar?
explanation: Ahmad Shah I (Wali, 1422-36) annexed Warangal and moved the Bahmani capital from Gulbarga to Bidar. Firoz Shah was his predecessor; Muhammad Shah III's era is Mahmud Gawan's.

notes.text: - **Kingdom:** **Malik Sarwar** (Khwaja Jahan, title **Malik-us-Sharq**, "Lord of the East") made it independent in **1394**; **Jaunpur** was the Sharqi capital.

q: Who founded the Bahmani Empire?
explanation: Hasan Gangu (Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah) founded the Bahmani kingdom in 1347 with Gulbarga as capital. Yusuf Adil Khan founded Bijapur; Prolaya Nayaka was a Musunuri chief.

notes.text: - **City:** founded by **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**, named after his cousin **Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Jauna Khan)**.

q: Who among the following founded the Bahmani kingdom in the Deccan in the 14th century A.D.?
explanation: Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu), a Tughlaq officer, revolted against Muhammad bin Tughlaq and founded the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347.

notes.text: - **City:** founded by **Firoz Shah Tughlaq**, named after his cousin **Muhammad bin Tughlaq (Jauna Khan)**.

q: In which war was gunpowder used for the first time in India?
explanation: The earliest recorded use of gunpowder weapons in India is by the Bahmani Sultan Muhammad Shah I against Vijayanagara (Bukka I), c. 1366-68 (Mudgal/Adoni). The Kakatiyas and Warangal were gone by then; Babur's Panipat (1526) only popularised field artillery.
